review:
Superhot is a fast-paced puzzle rather than just an FPS game. Its famous motto spoken at the beginning summarizes everything: "Time moves only when you move." Thanks to this simple mechanic, the game sets itself apart from combat and action games, turning into a Matrix simulation where we dodge bullets. The game generally takes place in minimalist environments. White rooms, red enemies, and black weapons. A simple, easy on the eyes, and memorable atmosphere.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3678922547
[h2] Story and Gameplay [/h2]

Every step we take is a decision, and every bullet is a risk. We can even stop a bullet floating in mid-air with our gun, which is one of the elements deepening the gameplay. While playing the game, it feels like we are playing chess. We must make every move carefully, and additionally, we need to analyze our surroundings thoroughly. While clearing enemies ahead of us, threats suddenly appearing from behind or from our right can ruin our entire plan. In fact, it sends a message that the more we try, the more flawless it becomes. With every mistake, we learn something new and act with more experience the next time.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3678921643
Even though the game's story is short, it is quite striking. We are a user sitting in front of a computer. We log into the game via an old operating system. Let's not forget that our friend recommended this game, well, at least that's what we thought... After playing for a bit, we realize this is not just a game, but a kind of mind data transfer protocol. Although the game tries to kick us out early on, we have already become addicted to it. At times the system challenges us, at times it belittles us, and even orders us to quit the game. I want to mention a neat detail here. When it tells us to quit and we refuse and keep playing, we get kicked out of the game, which surprised me a bit. When we launch it again, it says things like "you're not going to give up, are you?" and lets us continue.

One of the striking parts of the story is the phrase "MIND IS SOFTWARE - BODIES ARE DISPOSABLE". The system tries to sever us from our physical body in the real world and turn us entirely into a digital soldier. Past a certain point, the game tries to scare us by claiming it knows our real-world room. After a while, the game symbolizes an addiction loop. It does not force us to stay inside, in fact, as I mentioned, it even tries to throw us out up to a point. In the end, we are no longer a player, but a part of the system. We trigger the finale by shooting our own body. ONE OF US.

[h3] The fourth wall is broken multiple times in the game, such details are great. Even though it finishes in around 2 hours, it is a very memorable experience. [/h3]

[h1] Overall [/h1]

Steam really needs a review system that allows for more than just "Recommend" or "Don't Recommend", because I feel like SUPERHOT is, like many other games, neither good nor bad enough to be placed into one category. That said, this is ultimately a positive review, because I did have a good experience and most of my complaints are about a lack of getting more of that experience. It's the most innovative shooter I've played in years! But that doesn't mean it's without flaws.

First off, SUPERHOT plays extremely well. There's something about the slow-motion, time only moves when you do combat that is just inherently satisfying; if you don't believe me, there's a prototype/demo online (search "superhot demo" and you should find it) that will give you a taste. There's nothing too fancy aside from that, at least at first: just different weapons (pistol, shotgun, assault rifle, baseball bat/tire iron, katana), the ability to throw them, the ability to pick weapons up after punching an enemy to stun them (or hitting them three times to kill them). Later on you gain the ability to "hostswitch" from one body to another, but you only have it for a few levels.

The level design makes the gameplay all the better. While the earlier levels are either easy to beat on your first try or have an obvious, clearly placed solution, the game very quickly moves to a point where most levels take a few tries to beat. The game feels almost like a puzzle. Since ammunition is not unlimited and you'll often run out of bullets before you run out of heads to put them in, you have to conserve it as best you can while trying to make your way to the next gun. Since every punch or bullet will kill you instantly, but bullets move slow enough for you to dodge them and you can always hit an enemy before they're in range to do the same, you have to engage in a slow dance-like movement occasionally, carefully sidestepping oncoming bullets and beating down nearby enemies before they can attack. Even looking around consumes precious time, meaning that on some occasions you can't even aim at an enemy without giving another one time to shoot. (Here's looking at you, elevator level.)

The story... see, this is where the bad parts of SUPERHOT come into play. The story is actually an interesting idea, but you don't get even close to enough of it for them to properly deliver. Which wouldn't be so bad, if the story didn't take control of the game for long periods of time, preventing you from bashing in red polygonal men's heads in favour of watching a story that starts off intentionally obscured and almost pretentious. But right as it starts to seemingly expand on that, the game... well, the game ends.

The complaint many people have about SUPERHOT is that it's too short, and I think that is an entirely reasonable complaint. The gameplay is fun, but just as they start to move out of tutorialized levels to begin to combine the tricks they've taught you into interesting challenges, it ends in a climactic fight. Enjoyable, difficult, calling back to previous things you've learned, but ultimately... well, the end.

It feels like SUPERHOT is the tutorial to a much greater game. The story gets interesting; in the final "cutscene" (they aren't really cutscenes, but they serve the same purpose). The levels become sprawling arenas and headscratching puzzles; in the final segment. I beat the game in under two hours. I'll be the first person to say that length isn't everything about a game - I have played many games that I beat in similar amounts of time, and some of them are ones I consider masterpieces - but SUPERHOT is not a movie-in-game-form, nor is the gameplay explored well enough to leave me satisfied.

I think it really comes down to whether or not you're willing to pay as much as they're asking. I paid $21 CAD when it was on sale (40% down from $35). Is that worth a little under 2 hours of enjoyment? That's up to you to decide, but consider this: of my favourite games of all time, quite a few were bought for about $20, or even less. Many more were more expensive, but also far lengthier.

Do I regret buying SUPERHOT?
No.

Do I think I would have bought it knowing what I know now?
I'm not sure.

SUPER. HOT. SUPER. HOT. SUPER. HOT. SUPER. HOT. SUPER. HOT. After playing a little over 6 hours, I think it's pretty safe to say that SUPERHOT is one of the most interesting games I've played in a while. There are a few flaws and an intimidating price tag, but it's worth your time if you get it on sale.

[h1]Graphics[/h1]

The visuals have gotten mixed reception, but I'm personally a fan of the art style here. It's simple without feeling lazy, like many other indie games when it comes to their graphics. Plus, I can't help but watch the red guys as they crumple to the ground after they were killed. It makes every kill feel ten times more satisfying. Overall, the art style is simple in a good way.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]

I'm not going to lie, this game is incredibly fun. It definitely deserves the title as one of the most innovative shooters in years, and surprised me with the amount of content post-campaign. Yes, the main story IS really short, but I'll get in depth with that in the "Replayability" section of my review. The gameplay mechanics are unique and really creative. Watching a replay of you after you die/win (depending on the mode) makes you feel really badass. I don't need to explain the gameplay much, as you can just watch a video of it and know what you're in for. I will say, however, that it was executed very well and is about as fun as it looks. Plus, when you beat the game, you unlock endless and challenge modes, which give the game much more to do after you finish the campaign. Let the videos speak for themselves with this section.

[h1]Story[/h1]

The game comes off as a "kill bad guys" sort of game, but as you progress through the main storyline, you'll start to notice the game getting increasingly suspicious, without getting into details. It gets increasingly interesting as you go on, and while some people find it kind of absurd or weird, I found it to be pretty good. I'm starting to notice an increase in games that break the fourth wall frequently and try to toy with your mind, examples being [i]Undertale[/i] and [i]Pony Island[/i] as some of the better ones. SUPERHOT doesn't get to levels of those two in terms of mindfucking, but saying that the plot is boring or underwhelming would be a lie. The ending is one of the most clever endings I've seen in a video game. Once I was brought back to the menu, I stared at the screen, slowly clapping because of how creative it was. To conclude, I am pleasantly surprised with the story here.

[h1]Audio[/h1]

There isn't much in terms of audio. Some music, but the game is usually quiet. It relies on sound effects and the constant "SUPER. HOT. SUPER. HOT." to make your ears happy. Not much to say here, to be honest. As I said, the game is pretty quiet, and the sound effects aren't all that noteworthy. The only thing you'd remember here are the two words that you should probably know at this point.

[h1]Replayability[/h1]

Okay, I understand that the storyline is very short. Some people have finished this game in about an hour or two. I'm not very good at this game, and I did take my time with some parts, so I finished it in around three hours. The story is very interesting, but it didn't leave much else to question. So yes, the main story IS very short and that is a problem with the game. However, with the endless and challenge modes I talked about earlier, you'll probably spend some more time with the game. Rather than feeling like filler content, I actually wanted to play more of the game because of how much fun the mechanics are. No, this isn't like Skyrim and you're probably only going to get a few more hours of content, but at least there's more to do post-game.

[h1]Verdict[/h1]

Overall, SUPERHOT is very different and I am overall satisified with the experience. There are a few flaws, but the pros definitely outweigh the cons, so I can recommend this game. Just be cautious with that $25 price tag and know what you're getting into if you do decide to buy it at that price.

SUPERHOT is a very interesting idea indeed - it's a series of short combat puzzles taking place in a permanent bullet time. There's a semblance of a story thrown in, but frankly its only purpose is just pacing gameplay artificially to make it last a bit longer - otherwise the game could be completed in about an hour. It has distinctive minimalist style graphics and overall is pretty fun and engaging experience, focused on planning instead of quick reflexes.

There are some obvious flaws - physics are quite crude, player movement is very basic and hit detection is sometimes clunky. Enemies never run out of ammo and never need to reload, and any empty weapon discarded by you is magically full again when they pick it up, but I guess some compromises had to be made in order to make missions not too easy to beat. The main downside is that the game is very short - consists only of 27 playable levels, but you can always play challenges and endless mode after clearing the 'campaign'. 

I feel that it could be even better and bigger - but it's still definitely worth checking out, especially given its reasonable price.

[h2]Superhot Review[/h2]

Superhot takes you on a mesmerizing adventure that you had never experienced before. It’s brilliantly made gameplay never lets you feel bored. Each level is an unfamiliar experience and a significant challenge. The content may seem less, but it opens up the possibilities after the completion of a story mode. With a million-dollar matrix theme, where time moves, only when you move, makes it worth your time. Shoot red polygon enemies using various caliber weapons, or use whatever object is near you. Punch them, slice them, shoot them, whatever you want, only make sure to stay alive.
 
[h1][b]Gameplay:[/b][/h1]
Fresh matrix theme gameplay with variation in each level. It does not bound you to follow a single perfect path of completing a level. Make your own way for a perfect run. The game starts with a short new-style intro where you and your friend are talking about a new action game (Superhot), and he recommends you to try it. Then you with your gaming equipment enter the world of superhot. Your only aim is to stay alive after eliminating all enemies. As mentioned before, time only moves when you move your body, aka moving your head or walking. During this process, you will dodge bullets, melee attacks, or maybe some vehicles approaching you. You can use melee, swords, baseball, improvised throw able weapons painted with black color (cups, billiard balls, pots), or a wide variety of caliber weapons ranging from pistols, shotguns, and assault rifles.

Some powers like body-switching add an ample amount of action to your gameplay. 31 story levels, endless mode, challenge mode, extras, and a co-op mode makes it enough content to enjoy. As the name shows, story levels will continue your story journey, and endless-mode is for people who like to achieve a high score and want to face an endless horde of enemies; co-op mode is just a split control single character mode. It has a good sound composition and a smart way of promoting the game at the end of the story. Play as a killing machine in a VR style gameplay, without a need for VR. It flawlessly ported for KBM and controller players. Superhot is definitely a must-try game because of how smooth it feels and how the difficulty progresses throughout successive levels.

[h1][b]Graphics:[/b][/h1]
Even with a limited color pallet of three colors- White, red, and black, the graphics look satisfactory and amusing. Pleasing text font appearance with good on-screen animations keeps you immersed in the game. All the levels are bright and make you focus on the enemies and weapon only. Animations ranging from polygon shattering, weapon recoils, scene switch, and bullet trajectory are all perfectly developed. You will see great level designing over the scenes in an office, on a construction site, a parking lot, and a high-speed train. You can experience this gameplay on a low rig too. Feeling proud about the completion of a level with action-packed performance? How about using the in-game replay option and show your skills to your friends?

SUPERHOT is one of those games where the central idea is so simple that it is astonishing nobody had properly built a shooter around it before. Time moves normally only when you move. Stand still and bullets almost hang in the air, enemies slow to a crawl and you are given a moment to consider your next action. You are not particularly durable, ammunition is limited and you're forced to live in a John Wick movie taking weapons, throwing whatever happens to be nearby and carefully moving between bullets.

What makes the game considerably more interesting, however, is how its mechanics connect to what it is actually about. Without spoiling the story, SUPERHOT and its deep meaning delves into media addiction and the increasingly parasitic relationship between a game and the person playing it. It gives you something immediately satisfying and then repeatedly encourages you to continue consuming it until you hear another repetition of:

SUPER. HOT.
SUPER. HOT.
SUPER. HOT.

The fun is not separate from the message itself as the fun is how the message reaches you. SUPERHOT understands that the most effective way for a piece of media to control somebody is not to force them to continue, but to make continuing so entertaining that they willingly surrender their time and attention to it. You keep playing because you are enjoying yourself, even while the game quietly asks how much control you actually have over that decision.

When SUPERHOT was released in 2016, this could have been interpreted as clever commentary on video games and media consumption. Roughly ten years later, it feels considerably more like a warning. Modern games have become increasingly designed around daily rewards, endless progression systems, limited-time events and other carefully constructed reasons to keep returning. The same applies beyond gaming, where social media and endless scrolling compete to occupy every unclaimed moment of a person's life.

SUPERHOT does not predict every one of these systems, nor was media addiction invented after its release. What it does understand remarkably well is the underlying transaction. The game wants your attention, and it will reward you just enough to keep receiving it. The relationship becomes almost parasitic as it feeds on your willingness to continue, while convincing you that continuing was entirely your own idea.

My only real difficulty is justifying the price of what is now a decade old and relatively short game. The central mechanic is excellent, but the game itself is relatively short. I would recommend getting it on sale if possible.

Despite that, I absolutely recommend SUPERHOT. It is stylish, mechanically inventive and far more thoughtful than its minimalist appearance initially suggests. It is a game about how difficult it can be to stop consuming something that was deliberately made to keep you entertained, which admittedly makes recommending it to somebody else rather ironic.

Truth is I'm a huge fan of this game. Despite a couple technical hiccups (which may not be actual bugs, given the nature of the game), the game is ridiculously fun and stylish as hell. Though SUPERHOT has really only one gameplay gimmick, it never grew stale. Killing a room full of red guys in impossible situations never got boring, and the game's narrative actually kept me very engaged.

Since time only moves when you do, the game feels very far away from any other first person shooter made before it. It's impossible to run-and-gun, you need to carefully plan your steps to dodge deadly projectiles, while also aiming carefully and lining up those perfect shots; with so little ammo, you can't afford to be careless. It's the freshest breath of air an FPS fan has been able to inhale for the last long while.

So why am I not recommending this incredible game?

The price.


I've defended games like Jazzpunk and McPixel, even Undertale, when faced with the criticism of a game being too short. I truly believe it's about the experience. But SUPERHOT has pushed my limit.
$35 Canadian dollars for a game you can potentially beat in a few hours?
It's not quite worth it.

Is SUPERHOT really the most innovative shooter I've played in years? I'd say so. Even if you ignore the time control mechanics, it has plenty of unique features that set it apart from other FPS games. It's like a mix of a shooter and a strategy game, where you need to plan out your attacks and react to new threats that appear in levels. There isn't anything else like it on the market.

SUPERHOT is an FPS where time moves when you do*. Levels are centered around killing enemies as they appear and navigating around threats using your control over time. Sometimes, you'll be ducking and weaving around bullets down a long hallway as you close in on enemies. In other occasions, you'll drop in on enemies (sometimes literally), ambush them, and fight off reinforcements sent to kill you. 

The levels have a lot of variety to them, making them fun to replay and explore. It's satisfying to try them again and see how many ways you can complete them. You can punch out enemies, shoot them, throw weapons at them to stun them, jump on them to crush them, trick them into shooting each other, and more. There aren't many unique weapons or attacks in SUPERHOT, but they all stand apart from each other.

*Remember when I said that time moves when you do? That's not really the case. Time moves very slowly even if you don't move, meaning that you can't just stand still and calmly plot out how you'll eliminate the next enemy in sight. This can be frustrating to deal with at first, but it keeps the game from getting too slow-paced. 

The story is a big meta-narrative on gaming and addiction. It's pretty interesting, but it's also on the short side of things. You can beat the main game in 2-3 hours on your first playthrough. Fortunately, SUPERHOT has more to offer after that. Completing the story unlocks endless arena levels and challenge runs of the storyline. Some of the challenges change up the gameplay in fun ways, like trading the ability to shoot guns for one-hit-kill throwing weapons. Others offer increased difficulty, like limiting you to your fists or making enemies react faster to you. The endless arenas also offer some variety, like giving you a time limit or making you race to get 20 kills.

Some aspects of the game's design are pretty confusing. Guns have no ammo counters, forcing you to guess how many shots they have left. The shotgun has two barrels, but it somehow can fire three shots. Looking around with the mouse makes time move faster, sometimes causing you to die as you look for enemies or try to grab a fallen weapon. You'll eventually get used to these mechanics, but they can be annoying when you have to restart a level because of them.

SUPERHOT is a fun, frantic, and satisfying shooter to play. However, I would not recommend purchasing it at full price. 25 dollars is a big asking price when the main story is so short. Unless you are sure you'll love the game and play through all of its bonus content, I would recommend waiting for a sale before buying it. Once you try it, though, you might find it hard to put down. It's an addictive thrill ride from start to finish.

I can't recommend it or not. The core gameplay is great, but there are a lot of problems. If you like the demo and would like to play with variations on it on ~25 levels, go for it. An extra gameplay mechanic gets chucked in halfway to spice things up a little. 

It's a lot like Portal in that it's a small, short puzzlish game with an excellent, original atmosphere and style, but it's nowhere near as polished.
Story is compelling and fun, but only 2 hours long. Half of the challenge modes are good, half are garbage, there's about 12 in total. Endless mode is fun but you don't have any rewards or goals. Time-trial mode is the same. What sealed the deal for me continuing to play was the secret-finding exploration mode. 

It's fun to start up and play one or two levels for 5mins.
Add a level editor and proper way to share them and this would be solid gold.

~~~ Here's all the problems that should be easily fixed ~~~

Endless modes and time-trial modes are lack-luster; it doesn't compare scores against friends or give rankings/grades. Stupidly, the first ~1.5 seconds of in-game time occur with the loading screen still up, so you have to begin blindly to get the best times, not that there is anything motivating you to improve your time past the single goal they give. Endless mode is fun, but the game gives you no milestones to aim for - all of the unlockables (timed endless modes) are unlocked by total kills ever rather than top score.

Irredeemable bugs:
There's a minigame that doesn't stop the music on exiting, leaving it looping over itself and forcing a restart. Some achievements are bugged, including giving me the "complete all time trials" achievement when I only did 5 of them. Worst of all, completion of the last level you do before quitting IS RANDOMLY NOT SAVED SO YOU HAVE TO DO IT AGAIN.

Graphics:
The brightness can be a bit difficult to look at sometimes.
Animations are janky, which is a bit weird because they literally only have one animated model.
It is also somehow jittery at times? VSync is broken and doesn't lock to 60fps. Level 21 is very laggy for no apparent reason.
Settings menu is pitiful, you have about 3 graphics options and can't change key bindings.

Gameplay:
Thrown objects will very occasionally bounce off or pass through enemies for no apparent reason.
Thrown objects move faster than bullets. If you shoot and immediately throw a gun, the bullet hits the gun.
I don't know why they don't have time completely stop, it makes for a much more precise experience.
When you land from a jump the screen gets a pointless and annoying/disorienting shock effect.
You can't really tell how much ammo your gun has left, reducing your ability to plan stuff.
The gun reload animation is shitty and you can't tell how long it has left until you can fire again.
The end-of-level replays aren't quite satisfying enough, they're still too slow.
If an enemy breaks something too close to themselves they get stunned, which is a bit lame.
